title: Vacancy
full_review:
As far as hoteliers go, Mason, the night manager of the dilapidated Pinewood Motel, makes Norman Bates seem like a pussycat.

The film in question, "Vacancy" (Screen Gems), is a scary but ultimately distasteful film about a bickering, estranged couple, David and Amy Fox (Luke Wilson and Kate Beckinsale, both in good form), whose car breaks down in the middle of nowhere. (We learn, incidentally, that their estrangement has something to do with a child who has tragically died.)

They're lost after David took a detour off the interstate, and they have little choice but to check into the questionable establishment until morning.

Mason, as creepily embodied by Frank Whaley, offers them a deluxe suite -- as they're the only guests -- though it turns out to be nauseatingly filthy and bug-infested. Before long, they're being menaced by mysterious phone calls, and violent poundings on their door and walls.

The noises stop after David complains to Mason, but when David then decides to play some of the videos lying near the otherwise nonfunctional TV, the tapes show helpless men and women being brutalized and murdered in that very room.

Sure enough, they discover the room is rigged with cameras, and figure out they're to be the stars of Mason's next snuff film. So they must plot their escape.

On the plus side, starting with the clever puzzlelike credits, and the Bernard Herrmann-like Hitchcockian score, director Nimrod Antel skillfully generates an appropriately queasy mood. There are indeed plenty of jump-out-of-your-seat jolts for those who enjoy a good scare.

And it only takes a few of those knocks on the wall, and the couple is ready to reconcile. It seems a night in a creepy motel works better than a marriage counselor!

However, the voyeuristic aspects of the story and the gruesome violence in those disturbing videos -- and later, when David and Amy find themselves face to face with Mason and his cohorts (yes, there are others) -- push an otherwise effective thriller into the offensive category. Also gratuitous are the nonstop expletives in Mark L. Smith's script, and they're used even before all the bad stuff begins.

The film has brief but brutal violence, excessive rough language and profanity, fleeting partial nudity, voyeurism and sadism. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
